read.sections.0.text.source: In 1950, a British scientist called Alan Turing asked, “Can machines think?” Then, computers were new, huge and slow, and very few places had one. On 31 August 1955, four researchers in the United States wrote a proposal. Two worked at a college and a university, and two worked at big companies. They asked for 10 people to study “artificial intelligence” together for two months. They hoped to find out how machines could use language, form ideas, solve problems and get better by themselves. They believed one summer could bring real progress. The researchers asked a private charity, the Rockefeller Foundation, for money, and it agreed. The project took place at Dartmouth College in 1956. It did not solve those problems. But the name from the proposal is still used today.
read.sections.0.text.back: In 1950, a British scientist named Alan Turing asked, “Can machines think?” At that time, computers were still new, very big and slow, and very few places had a computer. On 31 August 1955, four researchers in the United States wrote a proposal. Two people worked at institutions of higher education, and two worked at big companies. They asked for 10 people to study “artificial intelligence” (kecerdasan artifisial) together for two months. They hoped to find out how machines could use language, form ideas, solve problems and get better by themselves. They believed one summer could bring real progress. The researchers asked a private charity, the Rockefeller Foundation, for money, and it agreed. The project took place at Dartmouth College in 1956. The project did not solve those problems. But the name from that proposal is still used today.
read.sections.0.text.note: “A college and a university” as “perguruan tinggi” (institutions of higher education), since Indonesian has no everyday college/university distinction. The English name “artificial intelligence” is kept here with the Indonesian, because the reading says the proposal's name is still used.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: In 1950, a British scientist, Alan Turing, asked: can machines think? Computers were new, huge and slow. In 1955, four researchers wrote a plan. This proposal asked for 10 people to work for two months. They would study “artificial intelligence”. Could machines use language? Could they solve problems and get better on their own? The group hoped to do a lot in one summer. A charity, the Rockefeller Foundation, paid. The project was at Dartmouth College in 1956. It did not solve these problems. But we still use its name.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: In 1950, a British scientist, Alan Turing, asked: can machines think? Computers were still new, very big and slow. In 1955, four researchers wrote a plan. This proposal asked for 10 people to work for two months. They would study “artificial intelligence”. Could machines use language? Could machines solve problems and get better on their own? The group hoped to do many things in one summer. A charity, the Rockefeller Foundation, paid for it. The project was held at Dartmouth College in 1956. The project did not solve these problems. But we still use its name.

read.sections.1.heading.note: “Boom” as “masa ramai” (busy, lively times), as in the video's content note; “masa jaya” (heyday) or “ledakan” are other options.

read.sections.1.text.source: After 1956, researchers tried different ideas at the same time. Some wrote rules for computers to follow. Others built machines that learn from examples, like the perceptron, shown by the US Navy in 1958. Much of the money came from governments. In the United States, a military agency paid for AI work at universities such as MIT and Stanford. Some researchers made big promises, but real problems were harder than expected. Computers were slow, and there was little data. In 1973, a British report criticised much AI research, and Britain then cut funding for some of it. Expert systems, built from rules that experts gave, began in the 1960s. In the 1980s, companies and governments, including Japan's, spent a lot on them. These cost a lot to keep up, and their market fell in the late 1980s. Times like these, when money and interest fell, are called AI winters. Historians still argue about their exact dates and causes.
read.sections.1.text.back: After 1956, researchers tried different ideas at the same time. Some wrote rules for computers to follow. Others built machines that learn from examples, like the perceptron, shown by the United States Navy in 1958. Much of the money came from governments. In the United States, a military agency paid for AI research at universities such as MIT and Stanford. Some researchers made big promises, but real problems turned out to be harder than expected. Computers were still slow, and there was little data. In 1973, a British report criticised much AI research, then Britain cut funding for some of that research. Expert systems, built from rules given by experts, began in the 1960s. In the 1980s, companies and governments, including Japan's government, spent a lot of money on expert systems. Their upkeep was expensive, and their market fell in the late 1980s. Times like this, when money and interest fell, are called AI winters. Historians still argue about their exact dates and causes.

In the 1980s, firms paid for expert systems. These used rules from experts. They cost a lot to keep up. Their market fell in the late 1980s. These slow times are called AI winters. People still argue about their dates.

read.sections.2.heading.back: Data, chips and the return of learning from examples

read.sections.2.text.source: AI is one part of a bigger story. Computers, the internet and digital data each have their own history. AI needed all three. There were also big successes. In 1997, a chess computer called Deep Blue beat the world champion, Garry Kasparov, though it could only play chess. Machine learning, an idea from the 1950s, grew much stronger after 2010. The internet helped researchers collect millions of labelled photos, and graphics chips made the work faster. In 2012, a team at a university built a program that was much better at naming things in photos. Rules did not go away. Many tools today mix rules and learning. Today, teams in many places build AI, also in Southeast Asia.
read.sections.2.text.back: AI is one part of a bigger story. Computers, the internet and digital data each have their own history. AI needed all three. There were also big successes. In 1997, a chess computer called Deep Blue beat the world champion, Garry Kasparov, although that computer could only play chess. Machine learning, an idea from the 1950s, became much stronger after 2010. The internet helped researchers collect millions of labelled photos, and graphics chips made the work faster. In 2012, a team at a university made a program that was much better at recognising things in photos. Rules did not disappear. Many tools now combine rules and learning. Now, teams in many places build AI, including in Southeast Asia.

write.example.source: In 1955, the researchers hoped a small group could do a lot in one summer. They wanted machines to use language and solve problems. It took longer because computers were slow and there was little data. Some promises were too big, so money fell in the AI winters. Later, AI grew faster. The internet gave millions of labelled photos, and new chips made the work quicker. I think this shows that good ideas also need the right computers, data and money.

The internet gave millions of labelled photos, and new chips made the work faster. I think this shows that good ideas also need the right computers, data and money.

watch.summary.source: In this video, a host called Jabril and a robot called John Green Bot talk about AI. AI is already part of daily life. It suggests videos, finishes words as you type, and helps decide some things about money and jobs. People have hopes and fears about it. The video links the name artificial intelligence to a summer project at Dartmouth College in 1956. The scientists there were very hopeful. Some said machines would soon be as clever as people. But they did not know how much data and computer power AI needs. So for a long time, progress was slow. This is called an AI winter. Then computers became much faster, and the internet made huge amounts of data. That is a big reason AI has grown so fast.

But they did not know how much data and computer power AI needs. So for a long time, progress was slow. This time is called an AI winter. Then computers became much faster, and the internet produced very large amounts of data. That is one big reason AI has grown so fast.

This lesson does not discuss it. If the topic comes up, answer briefly and factually, and don't ask learners about anyone's personal life.

educatorNotes.0.source: For teachers who want more: from the 1960s to the 1990s, DARPA, a US military research agency, gave most US government money for AI research, at MIT, Stanford, Carnegie Mellon and elsewhere (National Research Council, 1999). The Lighthill report was submitted in March 1972 and published in 1973; it is often said to have caused Britain's first AI winter, but Agar (BJHS, 2020; link in the claim record) shows the Science Research Council then funded some kinds of AI and not others. Haigh (2024) argues the deeper winter came in the late 1980s, after an expert-systems boom that Japan's Fifth Generation project and DARPA's Strategic Computing Initiative helped pay for; Japan ended its project in 1992 (Computer History Museum).
educatorNotes.0.back: For teachers who want to know more: from the 1960s to the 1990s, DARPA, a United States military research agency, gave most United States government money for AI research, at MIT, Stanford, Carnegie Mellon and other places (National Research Council, 1999). The Lighthill report was submitted in March 1972 and published in 1973; it is often said to have caused Britain's first AI winter, but Agar (BJHS, 2020; the link is in the claim record) shows that the Science Research Council afterwards still funded some kinds of AI and not other kinds. Haigh (2024) argues that the deeper winter came in the late 1980s, after an expert-systems boom that Japan's Fifth Generation project and DARPA's Strategic Computing Initiative helped pay for; Japan ended its project in 1992 (Computer History Museum).

educatorNotes.1.source: The evidence is real: the Dartmouth proposal (31 August 1955; the $7,500 Rockefeller grant, and industry researchers paid by their firms, come from the National Research Council's 1999 history, not the proposal) and a dated timeline. Teach the proposal's hopes, the people and institutions behind it and who paid, not names and dates to memorise. Its own topics already put “neuron nets” (learning) beside programs that follow rules: the approaches overlapped from the start. A possible discussion: why might confident plans help researchers win money, and what happens when the results come more slowly?
educatorNotes.1.back: The evidence is real: the Dartmouth proposal (31 August 1955; the Rockefeller grant of 7,500 US dollars, and the industry researchers paid by their companies, come from the National Research Council's 1999 history book, not from the proposal) and a dated timeline. Teach the hopes in the proposal, the people and institutions behind it, and who paid, not names and dates to memorise. The proposal's own topics already put “neuron nets” (learning) beside programs that follow rules: the two ways already overlapped from the start. A possible discussion: why could confident plans help researchers get money, and what happens when the results come more slowly?
